title: CNN Image Classification on DICOM Data (Research Example)
description:
Research and education example. Not a medical device, not for diagnosis or clinical decisions.

Shows the technical building blocks of a medical image classification experiment with TensorFlow/Keras and pydicom:

  • DICOM loading: rescale slope and intercept, windowing (Window Center/Width or percentiles), MONOCHROME1 inversion, resize, normalization to [0, 1].
  • Removal of direct identifiers (patient name, ID, institution, private tags) before data enters an experiment. This is not a complete de-identification profile.
  • Two binary classifiers: a small CNN that trains on CPU in seconds, and transfer learning with an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 backbone and a new head.
  • Evaluation with sensitivity and specificity on a held-out split, and Grad-CAM heatmaps to inspect which image regions drive the output.

The tests use synthetic DICOM files and synthetic images (a bright blob as the "finding"), not patient data.
implementationSteps: Get a dataset with a license that allows your use, and approval where your institution requires it. Keep patient data out of the repository.
Remove direct identifiers with deidentify() or, better, a vetted de-identification tool, and split the data by patient, not by image.
Load each DICOM file with pydicom: apply rescale slope/intercept, window to [0, 1], invert MONOCHROME1 images and resize to the model input size.
Start with the small CNN to check the pipeline end to end, then switch to the ResNet50 transfer model with a frozen backbone.
Train with mild augmentation (small rotation, zoom, contrast; no horizontal flip) and early stopping on a validation split.
Report sensitivity and specificity on the held-out test split and choose the threshold for the trade-off your study needs.
Inspect Grad-CAM heatmaps for a sample of images to find shortcuts such as text markers or device artifacts.
Document data source, splits, metrics and known limitations; an external validation set from another site is needed before any claim about generalization.
performance:
Expectations, not measured results:

  • The small CNN trains on 160 synthetic 48 x 48 images on a CPU in well under a minute; the tests require at least 85 % accuracy on that synthetic task, which says nothing about medical images.
  • ResNet50 at 224 x 224 needs a GPU for training on real dataset sizes; inference on a CPU takes a fraction of a second per image.
  • Report sensitivity and specificity with confidence intervals on a held-out, patient-level split of a public or approved dataset.
userExperience: A researcher runs one command to train and gets a JSON report with sensitivity, specificity and accuracy. A Grad-CAM heatmap per image shows where the model looked. There is no clinical user interface: outputs are for experiments and teaching, not for patient care.
